title: Embedding model training
summary: Train independent query and document encoders so relevant pairs score higher than negatives.
why: Enables offline document indexing and low-latency approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval.
interview: Design batches that contain hard negatives without training on false negatives.
derivation: Each row of the BxB score matrix treats the matched document as positive. Other batch documents are negatives only if the labels support that assumption. Shared Siamese weights are a choice; asymmetric encoders can use separate weights.

steps.note: Pool with an attention mask; normalize if using cosine.
Temperature controls score sharpness and gradients.
Cross-encoder scoring and labels help detect false negatives.

traps: Duplicate positives in a batch create false-negative pressure.
Random negatives become uninformative once the encoder improves.
Evaluate with the deployed index and candidate distribution.
tradeoff: Bi-encoders are indexable; cross-encoders jointly inspect each pair but cost more per candidate.
code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

q = F.normalize(torch.randn(8, 64), dim=-1)
d = F.normalize(torch.randn(8, 64), dim=-1)
logits = q @ d.T / 0.07
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, torch.arange(8))
assert loss.ndim == 0 and torch.isfinite(loss)

explanations.title: Bi-encoder retrieval versus cross-encoder scoring
paragraphs: A query encoder maps each query to q [D]; a document encoder maps each passage to d [D]. Documents can be embedded before the query arrives, so retrieval becomes indexed vector search. Siamese encoders share parameters; asymmetric query/document encoders may use separate weights or instructions.

A cross-encoder reads a query and passage together and produces a relevance score. It can model token-level interactions but must run per candidate pair. A common pipeline retrieves many cheap bi-encoder candidates, then reranks a smaller set with a cross-encoder.

Dot product mixes direction and norm. Unit normalization makes dot product equal cosine similarity. Training similarity, index distance, normalization, and query/document preprocessing must match or rankings change.

explanations.title: InfoNCE and false negatives in a batch
paragraphs: For B paired queries and documents, create scores [B,B]. Row i treats document i as positive and other columns as negatives. Dividing by temperature changes softmax sharpness. Cross-entropy encourages the positive score to exceed competing scores; a symmetric objective can also train document-to-query direction.

In-batch negatives are labels, not guaranteed facts. Two queries may share a relevant document. Duplicate passages, paraphrases, or multiple correct answers create false negatives. Use duplicate filtering, multiple positives, or a loss that masks known positives.

Small temperatures amplify hard-example gradients and mislabeled negatives. Evaluate recall@k with a held-out retrieval set rather than comparing only training loss. Keep documents from the same source or time boundary out of inappropriate train/test splits.

explanations.title: A practical hard-negative mining loop
paragraphs: Start with known positive pairs. Retrieve lexical candidates with BM25 and dense candidates with the current encoder. Remove positives and duplicates, then use labels or a stronger cross-encoder to identify plausible irrelevant candidates and flag uncertain ones.

A cross-encoder cannot prove that a passage is irrelevant. Human review or stronger labels are valuable for ambiguous examples. Train on a mixture of easy and hard negatives so the model does not overfit a narrow artifact of one miner.

Rebuild document embeddings after an encoder change and version the index with the model and preprocessing config. Measure candidate recall before reranking; no reranker can recover a relevant passage missing from its candidate set.
